name: Mandara (Wandala)
overview: In the majority and indigenous around Mora, the Wandala founded an ancient sultanate, open to the Kanuri, Podoko, Mouktélé, Shuwa Arabs, Malgwa and Kotoko. Islamised, and organised into kingship, castes and age groups, they live from farming, livestock rearing, trade and crafts, and share a long migratory route with the Kanuri.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority and indigenous group, integrated with many neighbours whose languages it often speaks.
Wandala is also spoken in Kerawa and Nigeria.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The ancestral land belongs to them; its history is linked to Islamisation.
Having set out from Ichga-Kewe, they stayed at Kerawa and Doulo, and keep ties with these places.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kingship, castes and age structure society; the chief decides and issues rulings.
The woman avoids interacting with men; children talk freely with their parents.
Permanent trade groups: blacksmiths, butchers, weavers (fabrics and wrappers), griot composers.
Relations with neighbours mix alliances and traces of history.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family. Men more often marry outside the group.
Steps: engagement, gifts, marriage proposal, bride price.
The bride price and gifts mark the commitment, the kola serves as testimony; perfume is also offered.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Islamic religious life: Mouloud celebrated every year, neighbourhood mosque (machidi, from Arabic masjid) and prayer ground outside the village (bala sallah), which keeps the memory of the group.
Birth enlarges the group; death is a loss. The prayers of the night, of Friday and of festivals nourish the deceased.
Taboos: talking about sexuality, insults, accusation. Idolatry leads to expulsion, crime to prison.
Prayer, sacrifices and fasting guide decisions.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade, crafts. Women: trade, crafts, farming.
The land belongs to the chief; the neighbourhood chief passes on requests, and the applicant's intentions are examined.
Ancestral crafts: guns, hunting arrows, gabaga clothing, parade swords for chiefdom dances.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men: coloured gandoura, grand boubou, waistcoat. Women: three-piece wrapper with headscarf, kaba.
Traditional medicine remains widely used: effective, inexpensive, accessible.
Beauty: figure, cleanliness, complexion; for women, cleanliness and jewellery.
Courtship: dancing talent, conversation, gifts.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: ganga koura (tam-tam, drum, flute), baré (tam-tam), goussa, goulva, kakou.
Dances: algaita at weddings at the chiefdom, doubdo at nuptials.
Festivals: Mouloud, Ramadan, Tabaski.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Wandala followed the same migration route as the Kanuri and share with them, as with the Mousgoum, scarification, clothing and cooking.

sections.title: The names
items: Names depend on sex; some are drawn by lot from among chosen people.
The birth name does not change, but a second name is given out of respect; an elder is not called by his name.
Appellatives: Abba, Baba, Ouma, Dada, Oummi, Igueye, Démama.
The founding ancestor, Sougada, is “the conqueror”.

lessons.title: Who are the Mandara (Wandala)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Mandara (Wandala) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Mandara (Wandala) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Mandara (Wandala) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Mandara (Wandala) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Mandara (Wandala) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Mandara (Wandala) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority and indigenous group, integrated with many neighbours whose languages it often speaks. • Wandala is also spoken at Kerawa and in Nigeria. • The ancestral land belongs to them; its history is linked to Islamisation. • Having left Ichga-Kewe, they stayed at Kerawa and Doulo, and keep ties with these places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority and indigenous around Mora, the Wandala founded an ancient sultanate, open to the Kanuri, Podoko, Mouktélé, Shuwa Arabs, Malgwa and Kotoko. Islamised, and organised into kingship, castes and age groups, they live from farming, livestock rearing, trade and crafts, and share a long migratory route with the Kanuri.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Mandara (Wandala) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Mandara (Wandala)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Mandara (Wandala) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Mandara (Wandala) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Mandara (Wandala) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Mandara (Wandala) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)

steps.instruction: Kingship, castes and age structure society; the chief decides and issues rulings. The woman avoids interacting with men; children talk freely with their parents. Permanent trade bodies: blacksmiths, butchers, weavers (fabrics and wrappers), composer griots.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Mandara (Wandala), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Mandara (Wandala)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Mandara (Wandala), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Mandara (Wandala).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Mandara (Wandala), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Mandara (Wandala).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: millet balls, okra sauce. • Drinks: porridge, tea. • Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade, crafts. Women: trade, crafts, farming. • Ancestral crafts: guns, hunting arrows, gabaga clothes, ceremonial swords for chiefdom dances.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Mandara (Wandala) eat mainly millet balls, okra sauce. Traditional drinks: porridge, tea. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Mandara (Wandala): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Mandara (Wandala)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mandara (Wandala), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Mandara (Wandala). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mandara (Wandala), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Mandara (Wandala). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, livestock, trade, crafts. Women: trade, crafts, farming. • Land belongs to the chief; the quarter head passes on requests, and the applicant's intentions are examined. • Ancestral crafts: guns, hunting arrows, gabaga clothes, ceremonial swords for chiefdom dances.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade, crafts. Women: trade, crafts, farming. Land belongs to the chief; the quarter head passes on requests, and the applicant's intentions are examined.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Mandara (Wandala)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover how the Mandara (Wandala) make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify
activities.instruction: Classify the activities in a men / women table.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade, crafts. Women: trade, crafts, farming. Land belongs to the chief; the quarter head passes on requests, and the applicant's intentions are examined.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Mandara (Wandala)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mandara (Wandala), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Mandara (Wandala). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mandara (Wandala), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Mandara (Wandala). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Islamic religious life: Mouloud celebrated every year, neighbourhood mosque (machidi, from Arabic masjid) and prayer ground outside the village (bala sallah), which keeps the memory of the group. • Birth enlarges the group; death is a loss. Prayers at night, on Fridays and on festivals nourish the dead. • Taboos: talking about sexuality, insults, accusations. Idolatry leads to expulsion, crime to prison. • Prayer, sacrifices and fasting guide decisions.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Islamic religious life: Mouloud celebrated every year, neighbourhood mosque (machidi, from Arabic masjid) and prayer ground outside the village (bala sallah), which keeps the memory of the group. Birth enlarges the group; death is a loss. The prayers of the night, of Friday and of festivals nourish the dead.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Mandara (Wandala) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Mandara (Wandala) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: Islamic religious life: Mouloud celebrated every year, neighbourhood mosque (machidi, from Arabic masjid) and prayer ground outside the village (bala sallah), which keeps the memory of the group. Birth enlarges the group; death is a loss. The prayers of the night, of Friday and of festivals nourish the dead.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Wandala
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Mandara (Wandala) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Mandara (Wandala) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Mandara (Wandala) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Mandara (Wandala) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Wandala. • Greetings: Ousé = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Gombré = morning greeting (one person); Gombré wa = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Pallé, Bwa, Kigué, Oufadé, Ildibé. • The founding ancestor, Sougada, is “the conqueror”. • The Wandala followed the same migration route as the Kanuri and share with them, as with the Mousgoum, scarification, dress and cooking.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Wandala are the first steps towards communicating with the Mandara (Wandala). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Wandala.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Wandala are the first steps towards communicating with the Mandara (Wandala). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
